blockers.quote: you chase thoughts, start drama, and drama pays too
blockers.why: story #6: You seek thoughts and receive thoughts, so this use has no expectation/result gap.
blockers.fix: Change it to: “You start drama expecting proof that people care. Coins pour in from anger, but your friend’s row goes dark.”

blockers.quote: your friend from the chai stall, the one who always paid a little, has stopped
blockers.why: story #9: The person is unnamed and first appears at the loss, without warm beats at least two minutes earlier.
blockers.fix: Name the friend in the first jump and add two warm actions—for example, “Asha saves your chai and sends the metro notes.” At the cost beat, mirror them: her seat is empty and her ledger row stops.

blockers.quote: The running total of a life: who carried you, by the coin.
blockers.why: story #5: The lifetime jump merely follows the friend’s loss; the outline supplies no but/therefore connection.
blockers.fix: Replace with: “Because Asha’s row has gone dark, you stop farming coins and scroll backward through the ledger—one day, one year, your whole life.”

blockers.quote: The turn breaks the planted belief that the money says how much they care: you open Sent.
blockers.why: story #10: No earlier spoken line explicitly equates coins with care, so the reversal contradicts nothing already said.
blockers.fix: Plant the spoken line near the first totals: “Coins are care. At least now you can count it.” Mirror it after Sent opens: “You love Mom. Sent is nearly empty. Coins were never care.”

blockers.why: No new power rule after the halfway point: Bad thoughts counting is first revealed in a beat extending to 65%.
blockers.fix: State in the rule beat: “Every waking thought pays—kind or cruel—and the app names who had it.” Then the drama beat applies an established rule.

suggestions.quote: The running total of a life: who carried you, by the coin.
suggestions.fix: Make the montage concrete: keep the phone in the same hand as the hand ages, while rows stretch from days to years and each scale change reveals a different person carrying you.
Answer this in the rule beat with “Every waking thought pays,” before the question can distract from the story.

suggestions.quote: dead? Can I see who exactly? Why is mom so high?
suggestions.fix: The app already answers identity. Show why Mom is high through ordinary cutaways—packing food, checking the metro time, noticing your unanswered call—and remove the dead-person question unless the story will answer it.

keep.quote: expecting to be rich: your crush has paid nothing, and your mother pays every four minutes.
Night: coins dropping one by one at 2 a.m., every one from mom, a skyline of her bar over everyone else's
The phone face down. You call the friend; somewhere a coin we never see drops for him.
